reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: A dermal spindle-cell tumour of the sun-damaged skin of elderly patients, typically on the scalp, face, and ears
Presents as a rapidly growing, often ulcerated or crusted nodule on chronically UV-exposed skin
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring immunohistochemistry to rule out spindle-cell squamous carcinoma, melanoma, and leiomyosarcoma
Histology shows a dermal proliferation of pleomorphic spindle and epithelioid cells with bizarre mitoses but, by definition, no deep invasion or necrosis
Immunohistochemistry is typically negative for cytokeratins, S100/SOX10, and desmin, with support from markers such as CD10, though CD10 is not specific
Extension into subcutis, deep invasion, necrosis, or lymphovascular involvement reclassifies the lesion as pleomorphic dermal sarcoma, which is more aggressive
Complete excision, ideally margin-controlled (Mohs micrographic surgery), is usually curative for true atypical fibroxanthoma
reference.pathophysiology: Atypical fibroxanthoma is a superficial pleomorphic mesenchymal tumour arising in the dermis of severely sun-damaged skin, with ultraviolet radiation implicated as the principal driver through characteristic UV-signature mutations, notably in TP53. The lesion is composed of atypical spindled, epithelioid, and multinucleated cells with numerous, often atypical, mitotic figures. It is confined to the dermis and lacks the deep infiltration, tumour necrosis, and lymphovascular or perineural invasion that define its more aggressive counterpart, pleomorphic dermal sarcoma. Because its pleomorphic appearance overlaps with several malignant spindle-cell tumours, its diagnosis rests on excluding those entities immunohistochemically, and its indolent behaviour depends on the tumour remaining superficial.
additionalInvestigations: Excisional or deep incisional biopsy sampling the full thickness of the lesion
Broad immunohistochemistry panel including cytokeratins, S100/SOX10, and desmin to exclude mimics
Additional supportive markers such as CD10 interpreted with caution
Assessment of depth, necrosis, and lymphovascular invasion to distinguish from pleomorphic dermal sarcoma
Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision with margin control
Imaging if deep or recurrent disease is suspected
redFlags: Deep subcutaneous or fascial invasion, necrosis, or lymphovascular invasion indicating pleomorphic dermal sarcoma
Recurrence after excision suggesting incomplete removal or reclassification
Rapid enlargement or fixation to deeper structures
Regional or distant metastasis, which should prompt reappraisal of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: True atypical fibroxanthoma has an excellent prognosis after complete excision, with low recurrence and rare metastasis; prognosis worsens substantially if the lesion is in fact a pleomorphic dermal sarcoma, which carries a meaningful risk of recurrence and metastasis.
pitfalls: Diagnosing atypical fibroxanthoma without adequate immunohistochemistry to exclude carcinoma, melanoma, and sarcoma
Failing to recognise deep invasion or necrosis that reclassifies it as pleomorphic dermal sarcoma
Relying on non-specific markers such as CD10 as if they were confirmatory
Under-sampling a superficial biopsy that cannot assess depth of invasion
management: Confirm diagnosis is one of exclusion using a broad immunohistochemical panel to rule out spindle cell squamous cell carcinoma, desmoplastic or spindle cell melanoma, and leiomyosarcoma.
Wait for complete excision and full histologic assessment before finalizing a management plan, since a superficial or incisional biopsy cannot reliably exclude pleomorphic dermal sarcoma.
For localized true AFX confined to the dermis with no adverse histologic features, primary treatment is surgical removal with complete excision as the goal.
Both wide local excision and Mohs micrographic surgery are used; retrospective data favor Mohs for better margin control and tissue conservation, with lower reported local recurrence.
There is no established role for adjuvant radiotherapy or systemic therapy in histologically confirmed, completely excised, localized AFX; this stage is managed surgically.

If the excision specimen shows deep invasion, necrosis, or lymphovascular or perineural invasion, reclassify as pleomorphic dermal sarcoma and manage with more aggressive intent, including wider margins and closer surveillance.
No standardized systemic or radiation protocol exists for pleomorphic dermal sarcoma; individualize management.

For unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease, radiation therapy or chemotherapy may be considered, but there are no clear guidelines and conventional chemotherapy has proven largely ineffectual; do not present chemotherapy as a proven benefit.

Activating RAS pathway mutations found in some tumors make targeted molecular inhibitors a potential future direction, but this is investigational only, with no established agent or drug class to name as standard.
Refer unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic cases to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team for individualized decisions rather than following a fixed treatment algorithm.
Follow up after excision for local recurrence.
Increase surveillance vigilance in immunosuppressed or organ transplant patients, who have substantially higher reported recurrence and metastasis rates.
Maintain ongoing photoprotection and surveillance for other ultraviolet driven skin cancers in the same field, since these tumors arise on chronically sun damaged skin.
Arrange imaging if deep or recurrent disease is suspected, particularly to reassess whether the lesion should be reclassified as pleomorphic dermal sarcoma.
